prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff passenger.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the Montreal Convention's two-year limitations period is a condition precedent to suit that may nonetheless be affected by equitable considerations, or alternatively the airline's bankruptcy stay tolls it.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Montreal Convention's two-year period is a condition precedent to suit, but it is not immune from equitable considerations.**

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that the right to damages "shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air art. 35(1), May 28, 1999, S. Treaty Doc. No. 106-45, 2242 U.N.T.S. 309. Article 35(2) then provides that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seised of the case." *Id.* art. 35(2). Even if Article 35(1) is a condition precedent, Article 35(2) sends the court to forum law on how the period is calculated. In this Circuit, forum law on calculating a filing period includes equitable tolling.

This Court has long held that a limitations period is presumptively subject to equitable tolling. *Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1478–80 (11th Cir. 1993). That holding applied the Supreme Court's presumption in *Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs*, 498 U.S. 89, 95–96 (1990). The Court has applied tolling where a plaintiff was prevented from filing by circumstances outside his control, and it has stressed that the doctrine is used sparingly and requires diligence. *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271–72 (11th Cir. 1999); *Ellis v. Gen. Motors Acceptance Corp.*, 160 F.3d 703, 706–08 (11th Cir. 1998). It has also applied tolling to a period that Congress and the treaty-making power had framed in mandatory terms. *Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, 1261–62 (11th Cir. 2006). It has applied tolling to a passenger's suit against a carrier. *Booth v. Carnival Corp.*, 522 F.3d 1148, 1149–52 (11th Cir. 2008).

A "condition precedent" label does not by itself take a deadline outside this framework. The question is whether the text shows that the deadline is meant to be rigid. Article 35(2) points the other way, because it expressly leaves calculation of the period to the forum's law. Here the Plaintiff sued in the time the Circuit's tolling principles allow. He acted diligently, and he was prevented from filing by circumstances beyond his control, namely the carrier's bankruptcy and the stay that followed. At a minimum, the district court should not have dismissed on the pleadings without deciding whether equitable tolling applies.

**II. Alternatively, the automatic stay suspended the two-year period.**

Filing a bankruptcy petition automatically stays "the commencement or continuation of a judicial . . . proceeding against the debtor that was or could have been commenced before the commencement of the case." 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). A claim against the carrier for Montreal Convention damages is such a proceeding. This Court treats actions taken in violation of the stay as void. *Parker v. Wendy's Int'l, Inc.*, 365 F.3d 1268, 1271–72 (11th Cir. 2004); *Jove Eng'g, Inc. v. IRS*, 92 F.3d 1539, 1546–47 (11th Cir. 1996). A passenger who filed suit against the debtor carrier during the stay would have filed a void action. He should not lose his claim because he did not file one.

Congress addressed this problem in 11 U.S.C. § 108(c). Under § 108(c), if "applicable nonbankruptcy law" or an agreement fixes a period for commencing a civil action against the debtor, and that period has not expired before the petition was filed, the period ends on the later of its original expiration or 30 days after notice of the termination of the stay. Article 35 is such a period. It is fixed by an international treaty, which is law outside the Bankruptcy Code. The statute does not exempt periods that are conditions precedent, and § 108(c) is a federal statute that applies to the carrier's treaty-based liability. Under it, the time that remained when the petition was filed was suspended for the duration of the stay and then extended to at least 30 days after the stay ended.

The same result follows from the equitable principles discussed above. A plaintiff who is barred by federal law from filing has the strongest case for tolling. *See Justice*, 6 F.3d at 1479–80; *Booth*, 522 F.3d at 1150–52. Under either route, the Plaintiff's complaint was timely and should be reinstated.

**CONCLUSION**

The Court should reverse the dismissal and hold that the Convention's two-year period was tolled, either equitably or by operation of the automatic stay and 11 U.S.C. § 108(c).
